_meta.note: Scene-writing reference layer. Every event with a `source` is citable; see docs/WRITING_GUIDE.md before writing any scene text.

events.title: Birth in London
events.summary: John Dee was born in London into a family whose Welsh connections and later claims of British antiquity would matter to his self-fashioning.
events.significance: The event anchors Dee's later attempts to present himself as both a learned European and a counselor with British historical credentials.
events.source: Glyn Parry, The Arch-Conjuror of England: John Dee (Yale University Press), pp. 23-27; Deborah E. Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature (Cambridge University Press), pp. 26-28

events.title: Studies at St John's College, Cambridge
events.summary: Dee entered Cambridge as a young scholar and was trained in the logical, mathematical, and humanist disciplines that underwrote his later reputation.
events.significance: Cambridge gave Dee the institutional beginning for a career that would join mathematics, natural philosophy, instruments, and courtly utility.
events.source: Glyn Parry, The Arch-Conjuror of England: John Dee (Yale University Press), pp. 29-35; Deborah E. Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature (Cambridge University Press), pp. 26-30

events.title: Becomes a founding fellow of Trinity College
events.summary: Dee became associated with the newly founded Trinity College and taught logic and sophistry in a university culture dependent on patronage.
events.significance: The appointment shows Dee's early movement through institutions where learning, status, and powerful patrons were already intertwined.
events.source: Glyn Parry, The Arch-Conjuror of England: John Dee (Yale University Press), pp. 31-35

events.title: Studies and networks at Louvain
events.summary: At Louvain Dee entered a major center of mathematical, astronomical, and instrument culture, encountering figures and methods that shaped his technical authority.
events.significance: The Louvain period made Dee a European mathematical practitioner, not merely an English university scholar.
events.source: Glyn Parry, The Arch-Conjuror of England: John Dee (Yale University Press), pp. 38-42; Deborah E. Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature (Cambridge University Press), pp. 28-30

events.title: Lectures on Euclid in Paris
events.summary: Dee's Paris lectures on Euclid helped establish his continental reputation as a mathematical teacher and interpreter.
events.significance: The event anticipates the later Mathematical Preface and Dee's lifelong claim that mathematics mediates practical, natural, and metaphysical knowledge.
events.source: Deborah E. Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature (Cambridge University Press), pp. 28-30; György E. Szőnyi, John Dee's Occultism: Magical Exaltation through Powerful Signs (SUNY Press), pp. 155-181

events.title: Arrested under Mary I after astrological suspicion
events.summary: Dee's astrological and prognosticating expertise drew suspicion during Mary's reign, leading to imprisonment and examination.
events.significance: The episode shows how mathematical and occult expertise could become politically dangerous when tied to royal futures.
events.source: Glyn Parry, The Arch-Conjuror of England: John Dee (Yale University Press), pp. 48-58

events.title: Publishes Propaedeumata aphoristica
events.summary: Dee's Propaedeumata aphoristica presented aphorisms on celestial influence, rays, and natural causation.
events.significance: The book is central to seeing Dee's astrology and optics as natural philosophy rather than as a detached occult curiosity.
events.source: Deborah E. Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature (Cambridge University Press), pp. 98-102; György E. Szőnyi, John Dee's Occultism: Magical Exaltation through Powerful Signs (SUNY Press), pp. 155-181; Håkan Håkansson, Seeing the Word: John Dee and Renaissance Occultism (Lund University), pp. 274-289

events.title: Consulted around Elizabeth I's accession
events.summary: Dee's astrological expertise became useful at the accession of Elizabeth I, including the broader culture of choosing auspicious times and reading royal futures.
events.significance: The event marks Dee's transition from suspect calculator to potentially useful Elizabethan counselor.
events.source: Glyn Parry, The Arch-Conjuror of England: John Dee (Yale University Press), pp. 48-58

events.title: Publishes Monas hieroglyphica
events.summary: Dee published the Monas hieroglyphica, a dense symbolic work joining mathematics, alchemy, cabala, and hieroglyphic interpretation.
events.significance: The Monas became one of the major test cases for interpreting Dee's symbolic natural philosophy and later alchemical reception.
events.source: Deborah E. Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature (Cambridge University Press), pp. 76-90; György E. Szőnyi, John Dee's Occultism: Magical Exaltation through Powerful Signs (SUNY Press), pp. 155-181; Håkan Håkansson, Seeing the Word: John Dee and Renaissance Occultism (Lund University), pp. 289-301

events.title: Builds the Mortlake library
events.summary: Dee developed the Mortlake library into a working scholarly collection used for reading, consultation, writing, and social exchange.
events.significance: The library made Dee useful to visitors and patrons, while also making his intellectual life materially vulnerable to loss and dispersal.
events.source: William H. Sherman, John Dee: The Politics of Reading and Writing in the English Renaissance (University of Massachusetts Press), pp. 56-80; Deborah E. Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature (Cambridge University Press), pp. 20-28

events.title: Writes the Mathematical Preface to Euclid
events.summary: Dee's preface to Billingsley's English Euclid defended mathematics as a practical and metaphysical discipline mediating visible and invisible orders.
events.significance: The preface is one of the clearest statements of Dee's mathematical ideology and his claim for learned usefulness.
events.source: William H. Sherman, John Dee: The Politics of Reading and Writing in the English Renaissance (University of Massachusetts Press), pp. 80-116; György E. Szőnyi, John Dee's Occultism: Magical Exaltation through Powerful Signs (SUNY Press), pp. 155-181; Stephen Clucas, 'Pythagorean Number Symbolism, Alchemy, and the Disciplina Noua of John Dee's Monas Hieroglyphica', pp. 1-8

events.title: Composes Brytannicae Reipublicae Synopsis
events.summary: Dee's Synopsis organized the Elizabethan commonwealth as a field for learned counsel and reform.
events.significance: The manuscript shows Dee converting reading and classification into political advice.
events.source: William H. Sherman, John Dee: The Politics of Reading and Writing in the English Renaissance (University of Massachusetts Press), pp. 216-277

events.title: Publishes General and Rare Memorials
events.summary: Dee's General and Rare Memorials advanced a program of navigation, maritime policy, and British imperial recovery.
events.significance: The work places Dee at the intersection of antiquarian history, navigation, print, and Elizabethan expansion.
events.source: William H. Sherman, John Dee: The Politics of Reading and Writing in the English Renaissance (University of Massachusetts Press), pp. 277-394; Glyn Parry, The Arch-Conjuror of England: John Dee (Yale University Press), pp. 114-138

events.title: First surviving angelic action
events.summary: The first surviving spirit action began Dee's extant record of angelic conversations, framed by prayer, discernment, and the search for divine wisdom.
events.significance: This marks the documentary beginning of the angelic project that later scholarship treats as central, not peripheral, to Dee's natural philosophy.
events.source: Deborah E. Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature (Cambridge University Press), pp. 35-42

events.title: Calendar reform counsel
events.summary: Dee participated in debates over calendar reform, where mathematical correction was inseparable from confessional and political caution.
events.significance: The episode shows that even technical expertise could become religiously charged in late sixteenth-century England.
events.source: Glyn Parry, The Arch-Conjuror of England: John Dee (Yale University Press), pp. 170-183; Deborah E. Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature (Cambridge University Press), pp. 155-159

events.title: Edward Kelley enters the angelic work
events.summary: Edward Kelley, initially known as Talbot, became Dee's principal scryer and the indispensable mediator of many later visions.
events.significance: Kelley's arrival transformed the angelic work into a long, unstable partnership of record, vision, obedience, suspicion, and dependence.
events.source: Deborah E. Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature (Cambridge University Press), pp. 35-40; Glyn Parry, The Arch-Conjuror of England: John Dee (Yale University Press), pp. 55-58

events.title: Heptarchical system takes shape
events.summary: The angelic actions generated the ritual and angelic materials that Dee later organized as De Heptarchia Mystica.
events.significance: The event matters because it shows visionary sessions becoming a structured ritual technology of names, offices, prayers, and objects.
events.source: Deborah E. Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature (Cambridge University Press), pp. 40-44; Håkan Håkansson, Seeing the Word: John Dee and Renaissance Occultism (Lund University), pp. 240-332

events.title: Leaves England with Albert Laski
events.summary: Dee, his household, and Kelley left England with the Polish noble Albert Laski, carrying the angelic project into Central Europe.
events.significance: The departure changed the angelic conversations from a Mortlake household practice into a project entangled with continental patronage and apocalyptic politics.
events.source: Glyn Parry, The Arch-Conjuror of England: John Dee (Yale University Press), pp. 183-200; György E. Szőnyi, John Dee's Occultism: Magical Exaltation through Powerful Signs (SUNY Press), pp. 241-281

events.title: Prague, Rudolf II, and imperial audiences
events.summary: In Prague Dee sought audiences and recognition in a courtly world fascinated by alchemy, prophecy, and occult philosophy.
events.significance: The Prague years show Dee as a public prophetic and political actor, not simply a private magus.
events.source: Deborah E. Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature (Cambridge University Press), pp. 20-37; Glyn Parry, The Arch-Conjuror of England: John Dee (Yale University Press), pp. 183-215

events.title: Revealed language, tables, and calls
events.summary: The angelic project produced revealed language, tables, calls, and names associated with later Enochian materials.
events.significance: These materials are central to scholarly arguments about Dee's search for a perfect or Adamic language and a true cabala of nature.
events.source: Deborah E. Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature (Cambridge University Press), pp. 199-213; György E. Szőnyi, John Dee's Occultism: Magical Exaltation through Powerful Signs (SUNY Press), pp. 181-241; Håkan Håkansson, Seeing the Word: John Dee and Renaissance Occultism (Lund University), pp. 309-318

events.title: Třeboň years under Vilem Rozmberk
events.summary: Dee and Kelley continued their angelic and alchemical work in Bohemia under elite patronage, while their partnership became increasingly strained.
events.significance: The Třeboň period concentrates the tensions among angelic obedience, alchemical ambition, household crisis, and patronage.
events.source: Glyn Parry, The Arch-Conjuror of England: John Dee (Yale University Press), pp. 200-226; Deborah E. Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature (Cambridge University Press), pp. 249-255

events.title: The communion of wives crisis
events.summary: The angelic records reached a crisis in the command involving Dee and Kelley's wives, one of the most controversial episodes in the corpus.
events.significance: The event reveals the extreme pressure that angelic authority could place on household order, friendship, obedience, and interpretation.
events.source: Glyn Parry, The Arch-Conjuror of England: John Dee (Yale University Press), pp. 200-215; Deborah E. Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature (Cambridge University Press), pp. 249-255

events.title: Returns to England without Kelley
events.summary: Dee returned to England after the continental project fractured and Kelley pursued independent alchemical patronage.
events.significance: The return marks the collapse of the Dee-Kelley partnership and the beginning of Dee's long struggle to recover status and support.
events.source: Glyn Parry, The Arch-Conjuror of England: John Dee (Yale University Press), pp. 226-238; Deborah E. Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature (Cambridge University Press), pp. 249-255

events.title: Mortlake library damaged and dispersed
events.summary: During Dee's absence and later decline, the Mortlake library suffered loss, damage, and dispersal.
events.significance: The fate of the library became a material symbol of Dee's vulnerability and the fragility of learned capital.
events.source: William H. Sherman, John Dee: The Politics of Reading and Writing in the English Renaissance (University of Massachusetts Press), pp. 56-80; Deborah E. Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature (Cambridge University Press), pp. 251-257

events.title: Appointed Warden of Manchester College
events.summary: Dee received the wardenship of Manchester College, an office that offered employment but placed him away from the courtly center he had long pursued.
events.significance: The appointment can be read both as provision and containment: a late-career office that did not restore Dee's earlier hopes.
events.source: Glyn Parry, The Arch-Conjuror of England: John Dee (Yale University Press), pp. 258-273; Deborah E. Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature (Cambridge University Press), pp. 251-257

events.title: Publishes the Apologetical Letter
events.summary: Dee's Apologetical Letter defended his reputation, listed his writings, and appealed against slanders of conjuring and unlawful magic.
events.significance: The publication is central evidence for Dee's late effort to control the record of his own learned life.
events.source: William H. Sherman, John Dee: The Politics of Reading and Writing in the English Renaissance (University of Massachusetts Press), pp. 15-56; Glyn Parry, The Arch-Conjuror of England: John Dee (Yale University Press), pp. 138-151

events.title: Late angelic actions
events.summary: A small set of late actions shows Dee returning to angelic communication near the end of his life.
events.significance: The late actions complicate any story in which the angelic project simply ended with Kelley or the continental failure.
events.source: Deborah E. Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature (Cambridge University Press), pp. 249-261

events.title: Death at Mortlake
events.summary: Dee died in poverty and diminished public standing, though his books, manuscripts, objects, and reputation continued to circulate.
events.significance: His death did not end the historical life of the materials: later editors, antiquaries, alchemists, and scholars remade Dee through reception.
events.source: Deborah E. Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature (Cambridge University Press), pp. 249-267; Glyn Parry, The Arch-Conjuror of England: John Dee (Yale University Press), pp. 273-322

events.title: Casaubon publishes A True & Faithful Relation
events.summary: Meric Casaubon published Dee's angel diaries within a cautionary frame about spirits, delusion, and unlawful curiosity.
events.significance: Casaubon's edition powerfully shaped later perceptions of Dee by making the angelic records public as a warning text.
events.source: Deborah E. Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature (Cambridge University Press), pp. 251-267; György E. Szőnyi, John Dee's Occultism: Magical Exaltation through Powerful Signs (SUNY Press), pp. 241-281
